En-dor
EN-dor
proper noun
Hebrew En-Dor, “spring of Dor” or “fountain of habitation,” a town of Manasseh, infamous as the dwelling of the woman with a familiar spirit.

Biblical Definition

En-dor was a town belonging to the half-tribe of Manasseh within the borders of Issachar and Asher, named among the towns Manasseh held but did not fully possess (Jos 17:11). It is remembered above all for the darkest night of Saul’s reign. When the king, forsaken of God and answered neither by dreams nor by Urim nor by prophets, sought a woman that had a familiar spirit, his servants told him there was such a woman at Endor (1Sa 28:7). Thither Saul went by night in disguise, to enquire of the dead what the living God would not tell him. The Chronicler sets down the verdict of heaven: Saul died for his transgression, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it, and enquired not of the LORD (1Ch 10:13). The dictionary marks En-dor as the place of forbidden enquiry, where apostasy reached its end in necromancy. The prophet Isaiah pressed the same reproof upon all generations: when men bid you seek unto them that have familiar spirits, that peep and mutter, should not a people seek unto their God? For the living to the dead? (Isa 8:19). En-dor stands as the warning that the soul which turns from God turns at last to the pit, and finds there no light at all.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Manasseh where the woman with a familiar spirit dwelt, the scene of Saul’s last apostasy.

EN-DOR, a town of the half-tribe of Manasseh, “the spring of Dor.”

It lay within the borders of Issachar and Asher.

There dwelt the woman with a familiar spirit whom Saul sought.

Forsaken of God, Saul came to Endor by night and in disguise.

It is the place where apostasy ended in forbidden enquiry of the dead.

Key Scripture

1Sa 28:7 — "Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor."

Jos 17:11 — "And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Bethshean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and her towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns, even three countries."

1Ch 10:13 — "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;"

Isa 8:19 — "And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?"

Modern Corruption

A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it warns that apostasy ends in the forbidden enquiry of the dead.

expand to see more

En-dor has met no redefinition from the present age, though the age is full of its spirit, seeking the dead and the hidden by every art the Scripture forbids. The dictionary records the town that the reader may know the end to which Saul’s apostasy ran.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the condemnation of necromancy and every traffic with familiar spirits. Saul, forsaken of God for his rebellion, sought the dead at Endor and died for it. The prophet’s rebuke stands over every séance and divination of the present hour: should not a people seek unto their God? For the living to the dead? The soul that turns from God turns at last to the pit, and finds there no light at all.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “spring of Dor,” En-dor names the town of Saul’s forbidden enquiry.
